summary: This RFC reproduces the executive summary of a National Research Council report comparing the DoD IP and TCP with ISO's internet and transport protocols. It was published to make that summary widely available quickly.

plainLanguage.summary: Experts compared two sets of network rules and wrote a short summary of what they found. This is that short summary.

questions: what did the nrc report say about tcp and iso

subtitle: A government committee compared TCP and ISO transport protocols for military networks.

tldr.problem: The Department of Defense had standardized on TCP and IP, but the International Standards Organization was developing its own transport and internet protocols (TP-4 and ISO-IP) that were incompatible. The DoD needed guidance on whether to switch.
tldr.mechanism: A National Research Council committee reviewed both protocol families and found them functionally equivalent in meeting military requirements. They evaluated the pros and cons of three options: immediately adopt TP-4 as costandard, demonstrate TP-4 first then decide, or continue with TCP.
tldr.outcome: The committee recommended adopting TP-4 as a costandard to gain the benefits of commercial products and external interoperability, though managing the transition carefully. The DoD ultimately moved toward TP-4 adoption over subsequent decades.

today: RFC 939 is a historical snapshot of a protocol transition decision. The DoD eventually moved toward broader adoption of TP-4 and ISO standards over subsequent decades, particularly as the Internet became dominant. However, TCP and IP remained the practical standard for most network communications, and TP-4 never became as widely deployed as originally anticipated. The tensions between TCP and ISO standards continued to influence networking decisions throughout the 1980s and 1990s.

sections.title: The Two Protocols
sections.content:
By the early 1980s, two incompatible transport protocol standards were competing for adoption. The Department of Defense had been using TCP and IP since 1978, and these were well-established and working across military networks and the ARPANET. Meanwhile, the International Standards Organization had developed TP-4 and ISO-IP as international standards for data communications.

Although TP-4 was partly based on TCP and provided similar services, the two protocols were not compatible. The U.S. government was supporting TP-4 as a Federal Information Processing Standard. This created uncertainty for the DoD: should they stick with TCP or transition to TP-4?

This RFC reproduces the executive summary of a National Research Council report commissioned to analyze the options and provide recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: There were two different rulebooks for how computers send data. The military had been using one, but the world was adopting a different one. Experts had to figure out which one to use.

sections.title: Military Needs
sections.content:
The DoD had unique requirements beyond ordinary data networks. These included survivability (networks must function even if many nodes fail), security (protecting traffic and data), precedence and preemption (prioritizing high-importance messages), robustness (handling unexpected loads and crises), and interoperability (different parts of the military being able to communicate).

The committee reviewed whether TCP and TP-4 could both meet these needs. The detailed comparison found that the two protocols were functionally equivalent: both could provide the required services, and neither was intrinsically superior in security or performance. Differences existed in data transfer interfaces, flow control, and connection handling, but none compromised military requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: The military needed networks that work even when things break, that are secure, that can prioritize important messages, and that let different commands talk to each other. Both protocols could do all of this.

sections.title: Maturity and Implementation
sections.content:
TCP had a significant head start in implementation maturity. Experimental TCP implementations were completed in 1974, and by the time of this report in 1985, TCP had been in large-scale operational use for years. The ARPANET switched completely to TCP in January 1983, and commercial TCP implementations were in use in private networks.

TP-4, by contrast, had not yet been implemented in any large operational system. It had been tested experimentally and endorsed by commercial vendors worldwide, and substantial portions were demonstrated at the National Computer Conference in July 1984. However, it was not yet available as a commercial product.

The report noted that the rapidity of progress in ISO standards had surprised even supporters, driven by market demand for integrated communications and data processing. The DoD networks had actually been a model for the ISO standards development.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP had been running in the real world for years. TP-4 was newer and was not yet in commercial products, but vendors were backing it and it looked promising.

sections.title: Three Options
sections.content:
The committee evaluated three strategic options. Option 1 (majority recommendation): Immediately modify DoD policy to specify TP-4 as costandard with TCP. New network proposals would prefer TP-4; existing TCP networks could continue, but the DoD would carefully review each case. The committee would develop military specifications for TP-4 and validation facilities.

Option 2: Announce intention to adopt TP-4 but defer final commitment until a satisfactory demonstration is complete. The demonstration would take at most 18 months. This option reduces risk but delays adoption.

Option 3 (not recommended): Continue using TCP and defer any decision on TP-4. Maintain awareness of TP-4 developments and work with NBS on data transfer between the two systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Option 1: Start using the new one now for new systems. Option 2: Test it first, then decide. Option 3: Keep using the old one and decide later.

sections.title: Trade-offs and Rationale
sections.content:
Option 1 offered the fastest path to commercial products and external interoperability with NATO and other organizations adopting TP-4. It would minimize the number of systems requiring conversion. However, it involved greater risk by committing to a new approach without as complete a demonstration.

Option 2 reduced risk through testing before commitment but involved higher transition and support costs due to more networks already using TCP. It also meant a longer period of operating with both protocols in parallel.

Option 3 eliminated transition costs and risks, provided rapid internal DoD interoperability, and kept the DoD in control. However, it meant higher procurement costs (commercial TCP products were more expensive than TP-4 would be), limited availability of implementations for new systems, and incompatibility with NATO and other external networks adopting ISO standards.

The committee believed all three options could meet DoD functional needs equally. The primary motivation for recommending Option 1 was to obtain the benefits of standard commercial products earlier, achieving cost savings estimated at 30 to 80 percent.
sections.plainLanguage: Option 1 is fast but risky. Option 2 is safer but slower and more expensive. Option 3 is safest but most isolated and costly in the long run.
